113.title: Holy, holy, holy (Isaiah 6:3)
113.hook: the preface ends and heaven and earth sing the same song
113.howItsDone: At the end of the preface, the whole congregation sings or says the Sanctus, joining the seraphim's words from Isaiah with the Palm Sunday Hosanna; in many churches everyone then kneels for the Eucharistic Prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the offertory: bread and wine carried up, and a drop of water in the wine. Your line was the ordinary is carried up. Which dull task did you carry? Day one hundred and thirteen.

About seven hundred years before Jesus, in Jerusalem, a young man named Isaiah goes into the Temple. And he sees something that nobody could paint properly. The Lord, seated on a throne, high and lifted up, and the edge of his robe filling the whole Temple. Above him stand fiery creatures called seraphim, each with six wings: two covering the face, two covering the feet, and two to fly. And they are calling out to each other, back and forth, so loud that the doorposts shake and the house fills with smoke. What they're calling is sung at every Mass, all over the world, today. Today's word is its name.
screen: `ISAIAH IN THE TEMPLE.` → `SERAPHIM WITH SIX WINGS.` → `THE DOORPOSTS SHAKE.`

segments.voice: Here's what they call, in the Douay-Rheims: "Holy, holy, holy, the Lord God of hosts, all the earth is full of his glory." In Latin, the first word is Sanctus, holy, and that's the name of this moment at Mass. In Hebrew, the word is kadosh, and it means more than good or pure. It means set apart. Other. Not like anything else. And Hebrew doesn't have an easy way to say most, so it repeats. Holy, holy, holy: the holiest there is. Now watch how the Mass gets there. After the gifts, the priest says: lift up your hearts. In Latin, Sursum corda. The people answer that they lift them up to the Lord. Then comes a prayer called the preface, giving thanks, and it always ends the same way: so we join the angels and all the saints in their song. And the whole church sings the seraphim's words. Then it adds a second line, from Palm Sunday. When Jesus rode into Jerusalem, the crowds shouted, in the Douay-Rheims: "Blessed is he that cometh in the name of the Lord." With Hosanna on either side. So in one short song, the Temple vision and the Palm Sunday crowd meet. And the idea is that this isn't a copy. The church isn't imitating heaven. For a moment, Catholics believe, heaven and earth are singing the same song at the same time. The same verse is at the heart of a prayer in the synagogue, the Kedushah, so Jewish neighbors sing it too. In the book of Revelation, the creatures around the throne never stop singing it, day and night.
screen: `KADOSH: SET APART.` · `HOLY THREE TIMES: THE HOLIEST.` · `LIFT UP YOUR HEARTS.` · `THE TEMPLE AND PALM SUNDAY MEET.` · then, large: `HOLY, HOLY, HOLY, THE LORD GOD OF HOSTS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: holy, three times. Settle, and breathe. If you pray, say the word quietly three times, with a slow breath between each. Holy. Holy. Holy. Let each one go a little deeper than the last. If you don't pray, think of something in your life that feels set apart: a place, a memory, a person. Something you'd take your shoes off for. Just hold it, and let it be other. The bell holds the time.
Sanctus. Latin for holy: the seraphim's song from Isaiah, sung at every Mass as heaven and earth join in. Today's word.
Your line: heaven joins in. Today, when you hear people singing together, anywhere, a stadium, a car, a kitchen, notice it, and imagine the song is bigger than the room. Day one hundred and thirteen.

options: that you must build a greater temple.
that you're a man of unclean lips, and undone.

what it means: the church singing the seraphim's song with them, heaven and earth at once.
what a scholar hears: kadosh repeated three times as a Hebrew superlative, the Trisagion of Isaiah 6:3, joined to Psalm 118's Benedictus via Matthew 21:9.

114.title: The consecration
114.hook: the words of Jesus are spoken and Catholics believe bread and wine become his body and blood (CCC 1376)
114.tomorrow: The Great Amen and the Our Father
114.howItsDone: During the Eucharistic Prayer the priest speaks Christ's words over the bread and wine, elevates each for the people to see and genuflects; bells are often rung, and in many countries the congregation kneels throughout.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Sanctus: holy, holy, holy, the seraphim's song. Your line was heaven joins in. Did you hear a song bigger than the room? Day one hundred and fourteen.

It's the quietest moment of the Mass. The singing has stopped. In many churches everyone is kneeling. Even the kids seem to know. The priest bends over the altar, holding a thin, round piece of bread in his fingers, and speaks words that are nearly two thousand years old. Then he lifts it high, above his head, so everyone can see. A small bell rings, or a set of bells, three times. He lowers it, and kneels. Then the same with the cup. If you've ever been in a church at that moment, you know the silence is different. Today's word is the long, strange name for what Catholics believe just happened.
screen: `THE QUIETEST MOMENT.` → `THE BREAD LIFTED HIGH.` → `A BELL, AND SILENCE.`

segments.voice: First, the words. At the Last Supper, Luke says, Jesus took bread, gave thanks, broke it, and gave it to his friends, saying, in the Douay-Rheims: "This is my body, which is given for you. Do this for a commemoration of me." Then the cup: his blood, of the new covenant. At the consecration, the priest repeats those words, not as a story about Jesus, but in the first person, as Christ. Now the belief. Catholics believe that at those words, by the power of the Holy Spirit, the bread and wine truly become the body and blood of Christ. Not a symbol. Not a reminder. Christ himself, really present. The name the Church gave this, in the Middle Ages, is transubstantiation. Trans, across. Substance, what a thing most deeply is. The Church teaches that the substance changes completely, while everything you can see, touch or taste stays the same: it still looks like bread, and tastes like wine. No chemistry changes. The whole reality does. That's why the bell, why the kneeling, why the genuflection after each elevation. Catholics often point to John's Gospel, where Jesus says, in the Douay-Rheims: "For my flesh is meat indeed: and my blood is drink indeed." Christians understand this meal in different ways, and it's fair to say so plainly. Orthodox Christians also believe the bread and wine truly become Christ's body and blood, and usually prefer not to explain how. Lutherans believe Christ is truly present, without this Catholic explanation. Many other Protestants understand the meal as a memorial, or a spiritual presence. For Catholics, it's the center of everything.
screen: `THIS IS MY BODY.` · `REALLY PRESENT, NOT A SYMBOL.` · `THE SUBSTANCE CHANGES, NOT THE LOOK.` · `OTHER CHRISTIANS SEE IT DIFFERENTLY.` · then, large: `DO THIS FOR A COMMEMORATION OF ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: one minute of stillness. If you're Catholic, or you'd like to, you can kneel. If not, sit up and let your hands rest open in your lap. Settle, and breathe. Picture the moment in that church: the bread lifted, the bell, the silence that follows. Don't try to think anything about it. Just be as still as that room. If you pray, you can simply be present to the one who, Catholics believe, is present there. The bell holds the time.
Transubstantiation. The Catholic name for the change of bread and wine into the body and blood of Christ, while their appearance stays the same. Today's word.
Your line: this is my body. Today, at your next meal, before the first bite, stop for three seconds of silence, the way a church goes quiet. Day one hundred and fourteen.

what a scholar hears: used at the Fourth Lateran Council in 1215, explained by Aquinas with Aristotle's substance and accidents, and defined at Trent (CCC 1376).

115.title: The Great Amen and the Our Father
115.word: The Great Amen and the Our Fathe
115.hook: the whole church says one loud Amen, then his own prayer
115.carry: so be it, all of us
115.howItsDone: At the end of the Eucharistic Prayer the priest raises the consecrated bread and chalice and the congregation responds with the Great Amen, often sung; then all stand to pray the Lord's Prayer, followed by the priest's prayer for peace and the people's closing doxology.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the consecration, and the long word transubstantiation. Your line was this is my body. Did you keep three seconds of silence before a meal? Day one hundred and fifteen.

Around the year 155, a Christian teacher in Rome named Justin wrote a letter to the emperor. People were spreading rumors about what Christians did at their secret gatherings, and he wanted to set the record straight. So he described a Sunday. They meet, he wrote. They read from the apostles and the prophets. Someone preaches. They pray. Bread and wine and water are brought. The one presiding gives thanks at length. And then, Justin says, all the people present answer with one word. He even explains the word for the emperor, because it wasn't Greek or Latin. It was Hebrew, and it meant: so be it. Today, that word, and the prayer that follows.
screen: `ROME, AROUND 155.` → `A LETTER TO THE EMPEROR.` → `ALL THE PEOPLE, ONE WORD.`

segments.voice: The word is Amen. It comes from a Hebrew root meaning firm, solid, reliable. At Mass, the long prayer over the bread and wine ends with the priest lifting both high, the bread and the cup together, and singing that through Christ, with him and in him, all glory and honor belong to the Father, in the unity of the Holy Spirit. In Latin, Per ipsum, et cum ipso, et in ipso. And the whole church answers: Amen. It's called the Great Amen, and it's often sung, sometimes three or more times. It's the people's signature on everything the priest has just prayed. Saint Jerome, around the year 400, wrote that in the churches of Rome the Amen rang out like thunder from heaven. Then, straight after, everyone stands and prays the Our Father together. In the Douay-Rheims it opens: "Our Father who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name." It's the one prayer Jesus taught his friends in his own words, and it's here for a reason. It asks for daily bread, just before the bread is shared. It asks to forgive, just before the sign of peace. At Mass, one thing is different. After deliver us from evil, the priest keeps going with a short prayer for peace and freedom from anxiety. Then everyone ends together: the kingdom, the power and the glory are yours, now and forever. Christians in many churches say that line straight after the prayer. Catholics say it here. First a whole church signs its name. Then it prays like a family.
screen: `AMEN: FIRM, SO BE IT.` · `THROUGH HIM, WITH HIM, IN HIM.` · `AN AMEN LIKE THUNDER.` · `THEN THE PRAYER HE TAUGHT.` · then, large: `OUR FATHER WHO ART IN HEAVEN, HALLOWED BE THY NAME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: one amen, meant. Settle, and breathe. Think of something you agree with deep down. A hope for someone. A thing you know is true. Something good you want to happen. Hold it clearly. Then, if you pray, say amen, out loud if you can, like a signature, not a murmur. If you don't pray, say yes to it instead, firmly. Notice the difference between agreeing and signing. Then sit. The bell holds the time.
The Great Amen and the Our Father. The people's loud so be it to the whole prayer of the Mass, then the prayer Jesus taught, said together. Today's word.
screen: `THE GREAT AMEN AND THE OUR FATHER — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: so be it, all of us. Today, when a group decides something good, a plan, a toast, a promise, be the one who says yes out loud. Day one hundred and fifteen.

what a scholar hears: Justin's First Apology 65 records the people's Amen around 155; the doxology after the Our Father is absent from the oldest manuscripts of Matthew, and the Mass places it after the embolism.

116.title: Lamb of God (Matthew 8:8)
116.hook: the bread is broken and all say Lord, I am not worthy, only say the word
116.howItsDone: After the sign of peace the priest breaks the consecrated host while the congregation sings the Agnus Dei; he then raises it with John the Baptist's words, and all respond with the centurion's words from Matthew 8:8, adapted to 'my soul shall be healed'.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Great Amen and the Our Father. Your line was so be it, all of us. When did you say yes out loud? Day one hundred and sixteen.

Remember the Roman officer, the centurion, back on day thirty-nine? His servant was sick at home. Jesus offered to come. And this powerful man, used to giving orders, said no. Don't come. I'm not worthy to have you under my roof. You don't need to come. Just say the word, and he'll be healed. Jesus was amazed. He said he hadn't found faith like that anywhere. Two thousand years later, every single time Catholics go to communion, just before they walk forward, they say that soldier's words. A pagan officer's sentence, placed on the lips of the whole Church. Today: the Lamb of God.
screen: `THE CENTURION, DAY THIRTY-NINE.` → `I AM NOT WORTHY.` → `HIS WORDS, ON EVERY LIP.`

segments.voice: After the Our Father, people turn and offer each other a sign of peace, a handshake, a nod, a hug for family. Then the priest takes the large host and breaks it. That breaking is so old that the first Christians called the whole Mass the breaking of the bread. He drops a small piece into the chalice, bread and wine together again. And while he does, everyone sings: Agnus Dei. Lamb of God. In Latin: Agnus Dei, qui tollis peccata mundi, miserere nobis. Lamb of God, who take away the sins of the world, have mercy on us. Twice. And the third time, instead of mercy: dona nobis pacem, grant us peace. Why a lamb? Because of John the Baptist. When he first saw Jesus coming toward him, he said, in the Douay-Rheims: "Behold the Lamb of God, behold him who taketh away the sin of the world." His listeners would have thought of the Passover lamb, whose blood marked the doors in Egypt the night of freedom. Then the priest lifts the broken host and says John's words, and the people answer with the centurion's. In the Douay-Rheims the officer says: "Lord, I am not worthy that thou shouldst enter under my roof: but only say the word, and my servant shall be healed." At Mass, one word changes. Not my servant. My soul. Catholics say it about themselves. It's honest: nobody earns this. And it's hopeful: you don't have to be worthy, only open. One word from him is enough.
screen: `PEACE, THEN THE BREAKING.` · `LAMB OF GOD, GRANT US PEACE.` · `JOHN SEES THE LAMB.` · `NOT MY SERVANT: MY SOUL.` · then, large: `ONLY SAY THE WORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: the centurion's words, for someone else. Settle, and breathe. The centurion didn't ask for himself. He asked for someone at home. Think of someone who needs healing today, in body or heart. If you pray, you can use his sentence with their name in it: Lord, I am not worthy, but only say the word, and they will be healed. If you don't pray, hold them in mind, and wish them whole. The bell holds the time.
Agnus Dei. Latin for Lamb of God: the song as the bread is broken, from John the Baptist's words about Jesus. Today's word.
Your line: only say the word. Today, notice where you feel unworthy of something good, and let it come anyway. Day one hundred and sixteen.

sources.ref: Order of Mass, the Agnus Dei (Latin)

117.title: Communion and the sending
117.hook: Catholics receive; others often come forward for a blessing; then go forth, the Mass is ended
117.howItsDone: Catholics who are prepared come forward to receive communion, answering Amen to 'the Body of Christ'; in many parishes those not receiving come forward with arms crossed for a blessing; after a closing prayer and blessing, the deacon or priest dismisses the people.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Agnus Dei, the Lamb of God, and the centurion's words. Your line was only say the word. Where did you let something good in? Day one hundred and seventeen.

Row by row, people stand and walk up the aisle in a slow line. An old woman with a walker. A dad carrying a sleeping toddler. A teenager in a hoodie. At the front, a priest or a lay minister holds up a small white host to each person and says four words: the Body of Christ. And each one answers with one word: Amen. Then something you might not expect. Mixed into the line are people who aren't receiving. They come up with their arms crossed over their chest, and the minister gives them a blessing instead. Nobody stares. Today, the last scene of the Mass, and the word for the whole thing.
screen: `ROW BY ROW, A SLOW LINE.` → `THE BODY OF CHRIST. AMEN.` → `ARMS CROSSED, FOR A BLESSING.`

segments.voice: Communion means union, sharing together. Catholics believe they receive Christ himself, so they prepare: at peace with God, having gone to confession for any serious sin, and fasting from food for an hour before. They receive on the tongue or in the hand, and sometimes from the cup too. That Amen is a whole creed in one word: yes, this is Christ, and yes, I belong to his body, the Church. Saint Augustine told new Christians something like: receive what you are, and become what you receive. Because communion is a sign of full unity in the Church, Catholics usually ask others not to receive. It isn't meant as a judgment on anyone. So in many parishes, anyone may come forward with arms crossed for a blessing. Afterward, there's silence. A last prayer. A blessing. And then the deacon or priest sends everyone out. In the old Latin: Ite, missa est. Go, it is the sending. That's where our word comes from. Missa became Mass. Christians have gathered for it every Sunday for nearly two thousand years, and for about sixteen hundred of them it has carried the name of its last line: you're being sent. It's the same root as mission. Look back over these two weeks. The entrance. Through my fault. Lord, have mercy. The Gloria. The readings, the Gospel and the homily. The creed and the prayers. The gifts carried up. Holy, holy, holy. The consecration. The Great Amen and the Our Father. The Lamb of God. And now, communion and the sending. The Mass doesn't end at the door. It's aimed at it.
screen: `COMMUNION: UNION, TOGETHER.` · `THE BODY OF CHRIST. AMEN.` · `A BLESSING FOR THOSE NOT RECEIVING.` · `ITE, MISSA EST: YOU'RE SENT.` · then: `FOURTEEN SCENES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan one kind thing after. Settle, and breathe. Picture walking out of wherever you are right now, out a door, into the rest of your day. Now ask: where am I being sent? Pick one person, and one kind thing you could do for them before tonight. A text. A favor. A patient answer. Be specific. If you pray, you can ask to be sent well. If not, just make it your mission for the day. The bell holds the time.
Mass. From the Latin missa, the sending: the whole Catholic liturgy, named for the moment the people are sent out. Today's word.
Your line: the Mass is a sending. That closes our walk through the Mass. Tomorrow, the rosary. Today, go and do the kind thing you picked. Day one hundred and seventeen.

screen: `DAY 117 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: HOW THE ROSARY IS BUILT.`

sources.ref: Catechism of the Catholic Church 1332, 1385–1398; Code of Canon Law 919 and 844

118.title: How the rosary is built
118.hook: the creed, an Our Father, three Hail Marys, then five decades each on one mystery
118.howItsDone: Catholics pray the rosary alone or in groups, often daily: the sign of the cross and the Apostles' Creed on the crucifix, an Our Father, three Hail Marys and a Glory Be, then five decades, each an Our Father, ten Hail Marys and a Glory Be while meditating on one mystery, often ending with the Hail, Holy Queen.

segments.voice: Yesterday, communion and the sending, and the word Mass, from missa, the sending. Your line was the Mass is a sending. What kind thing were you sent to do? Day one hundred and eighteen.

Hang around Catholics long enough and you'll see them. A string of beads wrapped around a rearview mirror. Wound around a grandmother's fingers in a hospital bed. Tucked in a soldier's pocket. Dangling from a teenager's wrist. Laid in the hands of someone in a coffin. Back on day ten, you met the beads. Now, for a week, we're going to open the rosary up and see how it actually works, bead by bead, and what people are thinking about while their fingers move. It's built like a small machine for prayer. Today's word is its main part.
screen: `BEADS ON A MIRROR.` → `IN A HOSPITAL BED.` → `A SMALL MACHINE FOR PRAYER.`

segments.voice: Start at the cross that hangs from the end. Holding it, you make the sign of the cross and say the Apostles' Creed, the one from day one hundred and one. Then, moving up, one big bead: an Our Father. Three small beads: three Hail Marys, traditionally for faith, hope and love. Then a Glory Be. That's the doorway. Now the circle. It's made of five groups of ten small beads, each group marked off by one bigger bead. Each group of ten is a decade, from the Greek and Latin for ten. For each decade, you name a mystery, a moment from the lives of Jesus and Mary. Then one Our Father, ten Hail Marys, and a Glory Be. The Hail Mary's first half is from Luke, in the Douay-Rheims: "Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee: blessed art thou among women." and "blessed is the fruit of thy womb." The second half asks Mary to pray for us, now and at the hour of our death. And the words aren't really the point. They're the rhythm. While the lips say the Hail Mary, the mind stays in the scene. Now, the name. Rosary comes from the Latin rosarium, a rose garden. Each Hail Mary like a rose, offered. And here's a lovely fact: the English word bead comes from an old word for prayer. People counted prayers on strings, and the word for prayer slid over to mean the little ball. There's an old story that Mary gave the rosary to Saint Dominic in the 1200s. Historians think it grew slowly over centuries. Either way, Pope Pius the Fifth set its familiar form in 1569.
screen: `THE CROSS AND THE DOORWAY.` · `FIVE DECADES OF TEN.` · `LIPS SAY, MIND STAYS IN THE SCENE.` · `ROSARIUM: A ROSE GARDEN.` · then, large: `HAIL, FULL OF GRACE, THE LORD IS WITH THEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: count ten. If you have beads, hold them. If not, you have ten fingers: that's a decade. Settle, and breathe. Touch one finger for each breath, slowly, all the way to ten. If you pray, you can say a Hail Mary on each finger, or just its first line. If you don't, let each finger be one calm breath. Notice how the counting frees your mind to rest. The bell holds the time.
Decade. A group of ten beads on the rosary, and ten Hail Marys prayed on one mystery. Five make a rosary. Today's word.
Your line: a garden of roses. Today, while you wait somewhere, count ten slow breaths on your fingers, one decade, and see what grows. Day one hundred and eighteen.

119.title: The joyful mysteries
119.hook: annunciation, visitation, nativity, presentation, finding in the Temple (Mondays and Saturdays)
119.howItsDone: Catholics pray the joyful mysteries of the rosary on Mondays and Saturdays (and often on Sundays of Advent and Christmas), meditating in each decade on the Annunciation, the Visitation, the Nativity, the Presentation, and the Finding in the Temple.

segments.voice: Yesterday, how the rosary is built: five decades of ten. Your line was a garden of roses. Did you count a decade on your fingers? Day one hundred and nineteen.

Think of the happiest stretch of your life. Not one moment. A stretch. A wedding and the months around it. A new baby in the house. A first apartment. Now notice: it wasn't all smooth, was it? There was fear in it too, and confusion, and at least one night you didn't sleep. But you'd still call it joy. When Catholics pray the rosary on a Monday or a Saturday, they walk through a stretch like that: five scenes from the start of Jesus's life, the stories you heard way back in the first weeks of Camp Two. They call them the joyful mysteries. Today's word is the second half of that name.
screen: `THE HAPPIEST STRETCH.` → `JOY, WITH FEAR IN IT.` → `FIVE SCENES, MONDAY AND SATURDAY.`

segments.voice: Mystery, in the rosary, doesn't mean a puzzle or a crime to solve. It comes from the Greek mysterion, a hidden thing that has been opened up. Something too deep to finish thinking about, that you can keep entering. Each decade is one of these, a door into a scene. Here are the five joyful ones. First, the Annunciation: the angel comes to Mary, and she says yes. Second, the Visitation: pregnant Mary goes to her cousin Elizabeth, and Elizabeth's baby leaps inside her. Third, the Nativity: the birth in Bethlehem, with no room at the inn. Fourth, the Presentation: Mary and Joseph bring the baby to the Temple, and old Simeon takes him in his arms, and also warns Mary that a sword will pierce her soul. Fifth, the Finding in the Temple: Jesus, twelve, goes missing for three days, and his frantic parents find him among the teachers. Now look at them again. A frightening angel. An unplanned pregnancy. A birth in a stable. A prophecy of grief. Three days of panic over a lost child. These are the joyful ones. The joy isn't the absence of trouble. It's what the story is doing underneath. And the rosary pictures Mary doing exactly this. After the shepherds' visit, Luke says, in the Douay-Rheims: "But Mary kept all these words, pondering them in her heart." That's the rosary: keeping the scenes, turning them over. Looking back over this week: the Sanctus, the consecration, the Great Amen, the Lamb of God, the sending, and now the beads. The Mass is the Church's great prayer. The rosary is a pocket-sized one.
screen: `MYSTERION: A HIDDEN THING, OPENED.` · `FIVE JOYFUL SCENES.` · `FEAR INSIDE EVERY ONE.` · `MARY KEPT AND PONDERED.` · then, large: `PONDERING THEM IN HER HEART.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: one joyful scene. Settle, and breathe. Pick one of the five. The yes. The visit. The birth. The old man with the baby. The lost boy found. Picture it as if you were standing in the room. What do you smell? Who's afraid? Where's the joy hiding? If you pray, you can begin a joyful decade on your fingers, Hail Mary by Hail Mary, and let the scene play. If you don't, just stay inside the picture. The bell holds the time.
Mystery. Not a puzzle, but a hidden thing opened up: a scene deep enough to keep entering. Today's word.
Your line: joy has a story. Today, look back at one happy stretch of your life, and notice the hard part that was inside it too. Day one hundred and nineteen.

original.note: Greek: a mystery, a hidden thing now revealed. in Latin it became mysterium and sacramentum.

trapdoor: what you thought: a mystery is something nobody understands.
